questionText: What are safe HTTP methods and why does the distinction matter?

target.learningOutcome: The learner can define safe methods from the effect requested by the client, list them, separate incidental server work from a business-state change, explain why automated retrieval depends on the distinction, and verify that a controller keeps the method's promise.
inScope: A focused read-handler versus command-handler example
outOfScope: A claim that a safe request performs no writes anywhere
A claim that every idempotent method is safe

claims.statement: A safe method has essentially read-only defined semantics: the client does not request or expect an application-state change as the result of applying it.
RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE as safe HTTP methods.
Safety does not prohibit incidental implementation effects such as access logging, because the client did not request those effects as the purpose of the operation.
Safe and unsafe methods are distinguished so automated retrieval, crawlers, link maintenance, and prefetching can operate without requesting harmful business actions.
When a URI parameter names an unsafe action, the resource owner must disable or disallow that action when the resource is accessed with a safe request method.
All safe methods are idempotent, while PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe because they request changes to application state.
Spring MVC uses GetMapping and PostMapping as method-specific mappings for GET and POST controller handlers; the handler implementation must still honor the selected HTTP method's semantics.

examples.title: Separate Spring handlers for reading and cancelling an order

validation.command: Review the two controller excerpts and their requested effects against Spring mapping behavior and RFC 9110 safe-method semantics
validation.expected: The GET handler only reads order state; the separate POST handler makes cancellation an explicit unsafe action

visuals.title: A safe order read, a destructive GET, and an explicit unsafe cancellation
Safe and idempotent are separate method properties

notes: The Spring cancellation route is an illustrative API design; the normative rule is that GET must not perform the unsafe action.
TRACE is listed because RFC 9110 defines it as safe, while the lesson separately notes that a server need not support every optional method.

review.notes: The definition, method list, incidental-effect boundary, automation rationale, destructive-query rule, and controller example were checked against RFC 9110 section 9.2.1 and Spring method-mapping semantics.
